title: 22. Interview: Design Netflix
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Netflix — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Netflix interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **Open Connect (custom CDN) vs AWS CloudFront**: Open Connect cost ~$0.005/GB vs CloudFront ~$0.085/GB. At 150 Tbps, that's $50 M/year vs $18 B/year. Netflix built Open Connect because the math was overwhelming. Trade-off: massive upfront engineering investment, but pays for itself in months.
- **Microservices vs monolith**: Netflix migrated from a monolith to 500+ microservices in 2010–2015. Pros: independent deployment, team autonomy, fault isolation. Cons: operational complexity, distributed transactions are hard, latency from network hops. Netflix picks microservices because team velocity matters at 9 000+ engineers.
- **Nightly batch vs real-time recommendations**: nightly batch is cheap and simple (one Spark job per region) but stale (24-h delay). Real-time is fresher but expensive (Flink per-event). Netflix picks hybrid — nightly batch + Flink real-time for "Continue Watching" only.
- **DRM per-device vs universal DRM**: studio contracts require DRM. Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady are device-specific. Trade-off: more engineering, but universal DRM doesn't exist. Netflix implements all three.
- **Cassandra vs Spanner**: Cassandra is multi-region, eventually consistent, open-source. Spanner is globally consistent, expensive, Google-only. Netflix picks Cassandra because they're AWS-locked and Spanner isn't available; they accept eventual consistency for most data.
- **HLS vs DASH**: HLS is Apple-native, broadly supported; DASH is more flexible. Netflix supports both — HLS for Apple devices, DASH for others.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why did Netflix build Open Connect instead of using AWS CloudFront?
**Answer:** Pure economics. Netflix streams ~150 Tbps at peak — ~15% of global internet traffic. At AWS CloudFront's egress price (~$0.085/GB), that's $50 M/day = $18 B/year — more than Netflix's total revenue. Open Connect is Netflix's purpose-built CDN: ~1 000 custom appliance servers embedded inside ISP data centers worldwide (free for the ISP — they save on transit costs because the traffic stays local). Each OCA is a 1U/2U server with 100+ TB of NVMe storage serving 40+ Gbps. Netflix pre-fills OCAs with popular content nightly (via scheduled "fill" jobs over cheap off-peak bandwidth). When a viewer presses play, the stream is served from a nearby OCA — typically within the user's own ISP — so the bytes don't transit expensive internet links. Open Connect cost is ~$0.005/GB (10–20× cheaper than CloudFront). Trade-off: massive upfront engineering investment (custom hardware, ISP partnerships, content placement algorithms) but pays for itself in months. Real-world: Netflix started Open Connect in 2012; it's the single biggest reason Netflix is profitable at scale. YouTube has the analogous Google Global Cache.
**Visual:**
```
Without Open Connect (CloudFront):
  150 Tbps x $0.085/GB = $50M/day = $18B/year (more than revenue)

With Open Connect:
  1000 OCAs embedded in ISP data centers
  Each serves 40 Gbps from local NVMe storage
  ISP peers with OCA for free (saves their transit cost)
  Effective cost ~$0.005/GB (10-20x cheaper)
  95% of bytes served locally, never hits AWS
```

### Q2. How does Netflix's recommendation system work at a high level?
**Answer:** Netflix's recommender is a hybrid batch + real-time pipeline. **Batch (nightly)**: a Spark job processes the previous day's viewing history for all 200 M+ profiles. For each profile, it generates ~40 personalized rows ("Trending Now", "Because You Watched X", "Top Picks", "New Releases", "Continue Watching", genre rows, etc.). Each row is generated by a specific algorithm — some are collaborative filtering (users with similar taste watched X), some are content-based (similar genre/cast), some are popularity-based (regional trending). The rows themselves are ranked by a model predicting which row the user is most likely to engage with. The output is cached in EVCache with a 24-h TTL. **Real-time**: when a user starts watching a new title, a Flink job immediately updates "Continue Watching" — no waiting for the nightly batch. **Cold-start**: new users get popularity-based rows for the first 2 weeks until enough history accumulates. Trade-off: nightly batch is cheap (one job per region) but stale; pure real-time is fresher but expensive. Netflix picks hybrid. Real-world: Netflix's recommendations drive 80%+ of watch hours — their recommender is a core business asset, described in their tech blog.
**Visual:**
```
Nightly Spark job (2 AM per region):
  for each of 200M profiles:
    fetch 90-day viewing history
    generate ~40 rows (each by a specific algorithm):
      - Continue Watching
      - Trending Now (regional popularity)
      - Because You Watched X (collaborative filtering)
      - Top Picks (NN ranker on embeddings)
      - New Releases, Genre rows, etc.
    rank rows themselves
    -> EVCache (24h TTL)

Real-time (Flink):
  on play event -> update "Continue Watching" immediately
```

### Q3. How does Netflix survive an AWS region outage with minimal impact?
**Answer:** Three layers of resilience. (1) **Multi-region active-active**: Netflix runs in 3+ AWS regions (US-East, US-West, EU-West, EU-Central, AP regions). Each region independently serves its users. Cassandra `NetworkTopologyStrategy` replicates critical data (viewing history, resume positions) across regions with RF=3 per region. If us-east-1 goes down, Route 53 detects it within seconds and reroutes traffic to us-west-2. (2) **Open Connect independence**: the OCAs are physical appliances in ISP data centers, not AWS. If AWS goes down, the OCAs keep serving cached video — only the API layer is affected. Viewers watching a movie keep watching; new plays fail until Route 53 fails over. (3) **Chaos engineering**: Netflix's Simian Army (Chaos Monkey, etc.) intentionally kills instances and injects failures in production daily. This forces every service to be resilient to instance loss (auto-scaling, retries, circuit breakers). When the real outage hits, the system has been "practicing" for it. Result: Netflix survived the 2017 us-east-1 outage (which took down many major services) with under 5 minutes of user-visible impact. Trade-off: multi-region active-active doubles infrastructure cost, but Netflix judges resilience worth it.
**Visual:**
```
3 AWS regions (active-active):
  us-east-1 <-> us-west-2 <-> eu-west-1
    Cassandra RF=3 per region (data replicated)
    Route 53 health-checks each region
    On outage: reroute to healthy region in seconds

Open Connect (separate from AWS):
  OCAs in ISP data centers keep serving cached video
  Only API layer affected by AWS outage
  In-progress plays continue; new plays fail over

Chaos engineering (Simian Army):
  Chaos Monkey kills instances daily in production
  Every service must survive instance loss
  -> "practiced" for the real outage
```

### Q4. How does Netflix's chaos engineering (Simian Army) work, and why?
**Answer:** Chaos engineering is the practice of intentionally injecting failures into production to test resilience. Netflix's Simian Army is a collection of automated "monkeys" that run continuously. **Chaos Monkey**: randomly terminates production instances during business hours. Forces every service to be resilient to instance loss — auto-scaling groups replace the instance, retries handle transient failures. If a service can't survive a single instance loss, Chaos Monkey exposes the bug before a real outage does. **Latency Monkey**: injects artificial network delays between services. Tests timeout and circuit-breaker behavior — services must degrade gracefully, not hang. **Conformity Monkey**: finds instances that don't conform to best practices (not in an auto-scaling group, missing monitoring) and terminates them. **Security Monkey**: detects security violations (open S3 buckets, missing IAM roles). **Janitor Monkey**: cleans up unused resources (orphaned EBS volumes, old AMIs) — saves cost. **Doctor Monkey**: detects unhealthy instances (CPU spike, disk full) and removes them. **Why**: traditional testing covers known failure modes; chaos engineering discovers unknown ones. Netflix's reasoning: in a distributed system of 500+ microservices, failures are inevitable — the question is whether the system degrades gracefully. By injecting failures daily, Netflix ensures the answer is "yes." Real-world: Netflix pioneered this in 2011; the practice has since spread to Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and most large tech companies.
**Visual:**
```
Simian Army (runs continuously in production):

Chaos Monkey    | kills random instances     | forces auto-scaling + retries
Latency Monkey  | injects network delays     | tests timeouts + circuit breakers
Conformity Mon. | kills non-conforming inst. | enforces best practices
Security Mon.   | flags security violations  | catches open S3 buckets, etc.
Janitor Mon.    | deletes unused resources   | saves cost
Doctor Monkey   | removes unhealthy inst.    | catches CPU/disk issues early

Result: system is "practiced" for real outages.
Netflix survived 2017 us-east-1 outage with < 5 min impact.
```

### Q5. How does Netflix handle DRM (Digital Rights Management) across devices?
**Answer:** Studio contracts require DRM — Netflix cannot stream without it. Three DRM systems are in use, each for a device family. (1) **Widevine** (Google): Chrome, Android, Chromecast, Android TV. (2) **FairPlay** (Apple): Safari, iOS, Apple TV. (3) **PlayReady** (Microsoft): Edge, Windows, Xbox. Netflix's playback service has a **DRM abstraction layer**: given the device type, it generates a per-session license token (JWT, 2-hour expiry) containing `profile_id`, `title_id`, `drm_type`, and `expiry`. The device requests the manifest (encrypted HLS segments) from the OCA, then requests the license key from Netflix's DRM license service (using the token). The license service validates the token, checks entitlement, and returns the decryption key (per-session, time-limited). The device decrypts segments as they play. **Rotation**: keys are rotated per-session, so a captured key is useless after 2 hours. **Offline downloads**: for mobile downloads, the license is bound to the device for 30 days. **Trade-off**: implementing 3 DRM systems is engineering overhead, but studios require it and there's no universal DRM. Real-world: every major streaming service (Disney+, HBO Max, Prime Video) implements the same 3 DRMs.
**Visual:**
```
Playback flow with DRM:
  1. POST /play/{title_id} -> playback svc
       -> generates JWT token (profile, title, drm_type, expiry=2h)
       -> returns manifest_url + drm_license_url
  2. Device fetches encrypted HLS segments from OCA
  3. Device requests license from drm.netflix.com/license?token=...
       -> license svc validates token + entitlement
       -> returns decryption key (per-session)
  4. Device decrypts segments as they play

DRM types:
  Widevine  -> Chrome, Android, Chromecast
  FairPlay  -> Safari, iOS, Apple TV
  PlayReady -> Edge, Windows, Xbox
```

### Q6. How does Netflix's adaptive bitrate streaming work?
**Answer:** ABR (adaptive bitrate streaming) is the same core idea as YouTube's HLS, but Netflix has additional optimizations. (1) **Manifest**: Netflix generates a per-device manifest listing available bitrates, audio tracks, and subtitle tracks. The same title may have 8+ video variants (240p–4K HDR × H.264/HEVC/AV1) + multiple audio languages. (2) **Player ABR algorithm**: Netflix uses a sophisticated algorithm (and recently, ML-based ABR) that considers not just current bandwidth but also: buffer health, predicted bandwidth (from history), screen size, device profile (mobile = lower bitrate default), and user's data plan (mobile data vs WiFi). The algorithm switches variants within 2 s of bandwidth change. (3) **Per-title encoding**: Netflix analyzes each title and assigns a custom bitrate ladder. An action movie with fast motion needs higher bitrate at 1080p than a talking-heads documentary. This saves 20%+ bandwidth without quality loss. (4) **AV1 for popular titles**: Netflix re-encodes top titles to AV1 (30–50% smaller than HEVC) — saves bandwidth at the cost of compute. (5) **Open Connect placement**: popular titles are pre-filled to all OCAs; the player is steered to the nearest OCA with the title cached. Trade-off: more variants = more storage but better user experience and lower bandwidth. Real-world: Netflix's per-title encoding paper (2015) influenced the whole industry; AV1 adoption is ongoing.
**Visual:**
```
Per-title encoding:
  Action movie (high motion): 240p=400kbps, 1080p=6000kbps, 4K=18000kbps
  Documentary (talking heads): 240p=300kbps, 1080p=3000kbps, 4K=9000kbps
  -> 20% bandwidth savings, no quality loss

Player ABR (Netflix ML-based):
  Inputs: current bandwidth, buffer health, predicted bandwidth,
          screen size, device profile, data plan
  Output: pick variant (within 2s of bandwidth change)

AV1 for popular titles:
  re-encode top 10k titles to AV1 -> 30-50% smaller than HEVC
```

### Q7. How does Netflix deploy 500+ microservices without breaking production?
**Answer:** Netflix's deployment pipeline (Spinnaker, open-sourced) is a multi-stage process. (1) **Bake**: build an AMI with the new service version. (2) **Test in canary**: deploy to 1% of instances in one region; monitor metrics (error rate, latency, CPU) for 10 min. If metrics regress, auto-rollback. (3) **Red/black deployment**: deploy the new version to a parallel "red" cluster alongside the current "black" cluster. Once red is healthy and serving traffic, switch the load balancer to red (black keeps running for 5 min as a hot fallback). If issues appear, switch back to black instantly. (4) **Multi-region rollout**: deploy to one region first; if it's stable for 24 h, deploy to the next region; finally, all regions. (5) **Independent deployability**: each of the 500+ services is owned by a small team (2–8 engineers) and can be deployed independently — no coordinated releases. (6) **Backward compatibility**: services must support N-1 version compatibility (new version can talk to old version) to allow rolling deploys. (7) **Automated rollback**: Spinnaker auto-rolls back if error rate exceeds threshold within 5 min of deploy. **Why this works**: small services + independent deploys + canary + red/black = a bad deploy affects 1% of users for 10 min, not all users for hours. Real-world: Netflix deploys thousands of times per day using this pipeline.
**Visual:**
```
Spinnaker pipeline:
  1. Bake AMI (new service version)
  2. Canary: deploy to 1% instances in one region
       -> monitor error rate, latency, CPU for 10 min
       -> auto-rollback if metrics regress
  3. Red/black: deploy to parallel "red" cluster
       -> switch LB to red when healthy
       -> keep "black" as hot fallback for 5 min
  4. Multi-region: one region -> 24h -> next region -> all regions
  5. Each service owned by 2-8 engineers, deployed independently
  6. Backward compat: N-1 version supported (rolling deploys)
  7. Auto-rollback if error rate > threshold within 5 min

Result: thousands of deploys per day, bad deploy affects 1% for 10 min
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A user reports a video keeps buffering on their smart TV. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Confirm bandwidth**: smart TVs often have weak WiFi. Ask the user to run a speed test on the TV (or on a phone next to it). Netflix needs ~5 Mbps for 1080p, ~25 Mbps for 4K. (2) **Check the OCA**: which OCA is the user being steered to? Check the playback service logs for the session — is the OCA hostname the user's ISP OCA? If not (steered to a far OCA), the OCA registry may have a stale ISP mapping. (3) **OCA health**: is the OCA saturated or degraded? Check OCA load dashboards — peak evening hours may saturate a popular OCA. (4) **Variant**: what bitrate is the player on? Check the playback progress events for `variant` field. If stuck on 240p despite good bandwidth, the ABR algorithm may be misreporting (a client bug). (5) **Title placement**: is the title cached on the user's nearest OCA? If not, the OCA fetches from AWS origin (5% case) — slow. Check OCA registry for title availability. (6) **DRM license latency**: if the DRM license service is slow, the player can't decrypt — appears as buffering. Check DRM service metrics. (7) **Device profile**: smart TVs have constrained CPUs; 4K HDR may stutter on older models. Suggest the user lower the bitrate in account settings. Most likely cause: weak WiFi on the TV, or the title isn't cached on the user's ISP OCA. Fix: steer the user to a different OCA, or pre-fill the title on the ISP OCA.
**Visual:**
```
Buffering on smart TV
  |
  +--> Bandwidth: speed test on TV (need 5-25 Mbps)
  +--> OCA selection: user's ISP OCA or far one?
  +--> OCA health: saturated? check load dashboards
  +--> Variant: stuck on low bitrate? ABR client bug
  +--> Title cached on OCA? -> check OCA registry
  +--> DRM license slow? -> check DRM service metrics
  +--> Device CPU constrained? -> suggest lower bitrate
  Fix: steer to better OCA or pre-fill title on ISP OCA
```

### Q2. Netflix is launching a new flagship show (Stranger Things S5). How do you prepare?
**Answer:** Anticipated launches need special handling. (1) **Pre-fill OCAs**: 24 h before launch, push the show's segments to all ~1 000 OCAs worldwide. This ensures every viewer's nearest OCA has the show cached — no origin fetches at launch. (2) **Pre-warm EVCache**: pre-generate the home page rows for all profiles with the show in "New Releases" — saves a thundering herd of cache misses at launch. (3) **Scale up API services**: auto-scaling groups pre-warmed to 2× expected launch traffic. Playback service, recommendation service, customer service all scaled up. (4) **Reduce ABR aggressiveness**: at launch, the player uses more conservative ABR (starts at lower bitrate, slower ramp-up) to avoid overwhelming the OCA. (5) **Region-rolling launch**: launch at midnight local time per region — US first, then EU, then Asia. This spreads the spike over 24 h instead of all at once. (6) **Multi-CDN fallback**: if Open Connect saturates in a region, fall back to AWS CloudFront (more expensive but available). Pre-configured in the playback service. (7) **On-call team**: the launch team is on-call for the first 6 h; if metrics regress, they can disable features (e.g., 4K HDR) to reduce load. (8) **Communication**: notify ISPs of expected traffic spike so they can provision. Real-world: Netflix has done this for every major release since 2016; Stranger Things S4 (2022) had 287 M hours viewed in its first week.
**Visual:**
```
Stranger Things S5 launch plan:
  T-24h: pre-fill segments on all 1000 OCAs
  T-24h: pre-warm EVCache (home page rows for all profiles)
  T-12h: scale API services to 2x expected traffic
  T-0:   launch at midnight local time per region
         - US first (00:00 EST)
         - EU next (00:00 CET)
         - Asia next (00:00 JST)
  T+0:   conservative ABR (slower ramp-up)
  T+0:   on-call team for first 6h
  T+0:   multi-CDN fallback ready (Open Connect -> CloudFront)
  T+0:   notify ISPs of expected spike
```

### Q3. A bad deploy breaks the playback service. How does Netflix roll back?
**Answer:** Spinnaker's red/black deployment makes rollback nearly instant. (1) **Detection**: within 5 min of deploy, Spinnaker monitors error rate, latency, and CPU. If error rate exceeds threshold (e.g., > 1%), Spinnaker auto-rolls back without human intervention. (2) **Rollback**: switch the load balancer back to the "black" cluster (the previous version, still running as a hot fallback for 5 min). This takes seconds. (3) **If after 5 min**: the black cluster has been decommissioned. Rollback requires redeploying the previous AMI — typically 5–10 min. (4) **Communication**: Spinnaker pages the on-call team with details of the rollback. The team investigates the root cause. (5) **Multi-region isolation**: if the bad deploy went to one region only (canary deploy), only that region's users are affected. Other regions are untouched. (6) **Circuit breakers**: downstream services have circuit breakers — if the playback service is failing, downstream services return cached manifests or default values instead of cascading failures. (7) **Post-mortem**: within 24 h, the team writes a post-mortem (root cause, timeline, action items) and shares it company-wide. Real-world: Netflix's red/black deploy was designed exactly for this — fast rollback is a feature, not an afterthought.
**Visual:**
```
Bad deploy -> playback service errors spike
  |
  +--> Auto-rollback (within 5 min):
  |      Spinnaker detects error rate > threshold
  |      -> switch LB back to "black" cluster (previous version)
  |      -> takes seconds
  |
  +--> After 5 min (black decommissioned):
  |      redeploy previous AMI (5-10 min)
  |
  +--> Multi-region isolation:
  |      bad deploy in one region only -> other regions untouched
  |
  +--> Circuit breakers: downstream services return cached/default
  |
  +--> Post-mortem within 24h, shared company-wide
```

### Q4. A new competitor (Disney+) launches and your CEO wants to add a "live sports" feature. How do you adapt?
**Answer:** Live sports is fundamentally different from VOD. (1) **Real-time ingest**: stadium cameras push RTMP/SRT to regional ingest endpoints. Latency to ingest must be < 500 ms. (2) **Real-time transcoding**: transcoder farm runs at 1× realtime, generating 4–6 bitrates simultaneously. Unlike VOD (where we can spend 10× realtime), live is bounded. Hardware acceleration (NVENC HEVC) is essential. (3) **LL-HLS / LL-DASH packaging**: 2-s segments (vs 10-s for VOD) to keep end-to-end latency at 5–10 s. (4) **CDN strategy**: Open Connect can serve live segments, but pre-filling doesn't apply (segments are produced in realtime). Each OCA fetches segments on-demand from the origin. Pre-warm the OCAs with the manifest URL. (5) **Fanout**: when the live event starts, notify users via push ("Your team is playing now"). (6) **Concurrency**: a Super Bowl may have 30 M concurrent viewers — 5× Netflix's normal peak. Scale OCAs and API services for the spike. (7) **DVR features**: pause, rewind — keep a sliding 4-h window of segments on each OCA. (8) **Ad insertion**: for ad-supported tier, server-side ad insertion (SCTE-35 markers, stitch ads into the stream). (9) **Multi-camera**: allow users to switch between camera angles — pre-encode all angles. Trade-off: live sports rights are expensive ($10 B+ for NFL); monetization is critical. Real-world: Amazon Prime Video streams NFL Thursday Night Football; Netflix streams WWE Raw (2024).
**Visual:**
```
Live sports pipeline:
  Stadium -> RTMP/SRT -> regional ingest (< 500ms)
  -> real-time transcoder (1x realtime, 4-6 bitrates, NVENC HEVC)
  -> LL-HLS packager (2s segments)
  -> Open Connect (segments fetched on-demand, no pre-fill)
  -> viewers (5-10s latency)

Features:
  - Push notifications at kickoff
  - 30M concurrent (5x normal peak) -> scale up
  - DVR: sliding 4h window on each OCA
  - Server-side ad insertion (SCTE-35)
  - Multi-camera (pre-encode all angles)

Cost: live sports rights $10B+; monetization critical
```

### Q5. A user reports they can't download a movie for offline viewing. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Device support**: downloads are supported on iOS, Android, Windows 10+ app — not on smart TVs or web. Confirm the user's device. (2) **Title availability**: not all titles allow downloads (studio contracts). Check the title's `downloadable` flag in the catalog. (3) **Storage**: does the device have enough free space? A 4K movie is ~6 GB. (4) **DRM license**: downloads require a persistent license (30-day). Check if the DRM license service issued the license — if not, the download fails. (5) **Network**: downloads need WiFi (Netflix blocks cellular downloads by default to avoid data charges). Check the user's network. (6) **Concurrent download limit**: Netflix limits to 100 downloaded titles per device, and a max number of concurrent downloads. Check the user's download count. (7) **Region restrictions**: a title may be downloadable in the US but not in EU (licensing). Check the user's region. (8) **App version**: old app versions may have download bugs. Suggest an update. (9) **Expiration**: downloaded titles expire after 30 days (or 48 h after first play). If the user is trying to play an expired download, it needs to be refreshed. Most likely cause: studio licensing restricts downloads, or the device has insufficient storage. Fix: suggest an alternate title or clear device storage.
**Visual:**
```
Download failed
  |
  +--> Device supports downloads? (iOS/Android/Win10+, not TV/web)
  +--> Title downloadable flag set? (studio contract)
  +--> Device storage enough? (4K = ~6 GB)
  +--> DRM persistent license issued? (30-day)
  +--> WiFi connection? (cellular blocked by default)
  +--> Concurrent download limit? (100 titles, max concurrent)
  +--> Region allows download? (US yes, EU maybe not)
  +--> App version current?
  +--> Download expired? (30 days, 48h after first play)
  Most likely: licensing restriction or insufficient storage
```

### Q6. The Cassandra cluster storing viewing history is at 85% disk and growing. How do you reduce storage?
**Answer:** Multi-pronged. (1) **TTL on old history**: add a 2-year TTL on `viewing_history` rows. Most users don't look at history older than 2 years; the recommender doesn't need it either (recency-weighted). Saves 50%+. (2) **Compaction**: switch from SizeTieredCompactionStrategy to TimeWindowCompactionStrategy — 40% reduction for time-series data. (3) **Compression**: enable LZ4 or Zstandard — 2–4× reduction. (4) **Archive cold profiles**: profiles inactive for 6+ months → archive their history to S3 (cheap, slow). Restore on next login. (5) **Aggregation**: instead of storing every play event, store aggregated stats per (profile, title, day). Drops 10× rows. (6) **Separate hot/cold keyspaces**: hot keyspace (active profiles, last 90 days) on fast SSD nodes; cold keyspace (older data) on cheaper HDD nodes. (7) **Vnode tuning**: reduce vnodes per node from 256 to 64 for faster repair. (8) **Audit for accidental inlining**: ensure no media URLs (just IDs) are stored in Cassandra. Net: 85% → 50% in a week. Real-world: Netflix has written about their Cassandra scaling challenges; TTL + TWCS + compression are the standard playbook.
**Visual:**
```
85% disk on viewing_history:
  +--> TTL 2y on history rows (-50%)
  +--> compaction: STCS -> TWCS (-40%)
  +--> compression: LZ4/Zstd (-2 to 4x)
  +--> archive cold profiles (inactive 6+ months) to S3
  +--> aggregate: per (profile, title, day) instead of per event (-10x)
  +--> hot/cold keyspaces: SSD for 90d, HDD for older
  +--> vnode tuning: 256 -> 64 for faster repair
  -> 85% -> 50% in 1 week
```

### Q7. A user reports their "Continue Watching" row hasn't updated after they watched an episode. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Did the play event reach Kafka?** Check Kafka for `playback-progress` events from the user's session. If no events, the device isn't sending them (network issue, app bug). (2) **Did Flink process the event?** Check Flink job lag — if backed up, events are delayed. (3) **Did Cassandra get updated?** Check `resume_positions` for the (profile_id, title_id) — is the position updated? (4) **Did EVCache get updated?** The "Continue Watching" row is cached in EVCache. Check if the cache was invalidated/refreshed after the play event. (5) **Client cache**: the user's app caches the home page locally — they may need to refresh (pull down on the home page). Check the app's cache TTL. (6) **Profile mismatch**: is the user watching on a different profile than they're viewing? "Continue Watching" is per-profile. (7) **Completion threshold**: if the user finished the episode (> 90% watched), Netflix removes it from "Continue Watching" and adds the next episode. Check if the completion logic fired. (8) **Region replication lag**: if the user is traveling, their viewing in region A may take time to replicate to region B. Most likely cause: the play event didn't reach Kafka (app or network issue), or the EVCache wasn't invalidated. Fix: have the user force-refresh the home page; if still wrong, replay the play event.
**Visual:**
```
"Continue Watching" not updating
  |
  +--> Play events in Kafka? (device not sending -> network/app bug)
  +--> Flink job lag? (events delayed)
  +--> Cassandra resume_positions updated? (position correct?)
  +--> EVCache invalidated/refreshed? (row cache stale)
  +--> Client app cache? (force-refresh home page)
  +--> Profile mismatch? (watched on profile A, viewing B)
  +--> Completion threshold fired? (> 90% -> next episode)
  +--> Region replication lag? (user traveling)
  Most likely: play event didn't reach Kafka or EVCache not invalidated
```
